glossary.definition: A number between 0 and 1 that measures how similar two pieces of text are by comparing the direction of their vectors. 1 means identical meaning, 0 means unrelated.
A number that measures the straight-line gap between two points in a vector space. Smaller distance means more similar.
A fast math operation that multiplies matching numbers in two vectors and sums the results. For normalized vectors, it gives the same ranking as cosine similarity but runs faster.

hook.scenario: Your embedding model turns 'dog' and 'puppy' into two arrays of 1,536 numbers. Before you read on, predict: which metric would a vector database use to decide which is closer to a query — the angle between the arrays, the straight-line distance, or both?
hook.question: Think about what 'similar meaning' means geometrically, then read on.

mental_model.intuition: Similarity is geometry — measuring how closely two arrows point in the same direction, or how far apart two points are in space.
mental_model.description: Once text becomes a vector, comparing meaning means measuring distance or angle. Cosine similarity checks if two vectors point in the same direction, ignoring how 'long' they are. Euclidean distance measures the physical gap between the two points. You do not need to memorize the formulas, but you must know which metric your model and database are using — because mixing them causes silent errors.

sections.body: Once text is embedded, it is a point in high-dimensional space. To find the best answers for a user's question, you need a math formula that turns two arrays of numbers into a single score saying how 'close' they are. The metric you choose defines what 'close' means.
sections.recap: You need a formula to turn two vectors into one closeness score.

sections.body: The standard choice is cosine similarity. It measures the angle between two vectors. If they point in exactly the same direction, the angle is 0 and the cosine is 1 — identical meaning. If they point in perpendicular directions, the cosine is 0 — unrelated. **Cosine cares entirely about direction and ignores vector length.**

image.alt: Left: two vectors with the angle between them. Right: two points with the distance between them.

sections.recap: Cosine = direction only. Two vectors pointing the same way = same meaning, regardless of length.

sections.body: Euclidean distance (L2) measures the straight-line gap between two points in space. It cares about both direction AND length. If two vectors point in the same direction but one is twice as long, Euclidean says they are far apart — while cosine says they are perfectly identical. For embeddings where length varies, this difference matters.
sections.recap: Euclidean = straight-line gap, sensitive to vector length.

sections.body: The dot product multiplies matching numbers in two vectors and sums the results. Here is the key insight: if your vectors are normalized (forced to have exactly length 1), the dot product gives the same ranking as cosine similarity. But dot product is faster for hardware to compute. This is why databases default to dot product when they know vectors are normalized.
sections.recap: Dot product is faster. For normalized vectors, dot product = cosine similarity for ranking purposes.

sections.body: **Most modern models output normalized vectors by default**, including OpenAI's `text-embedding-3` family. Because all vectors have length 1, cosine, Euclidean, and dot product all rank your results in the same order. In practice: configure your database to use dot product (inner product) for speed, and the ranking will be identical to cosine.
sections.recap: Pipeline: Text → Embed → Score (similarity metric) → Retrieve. For normalized embeddings, dot product is the fastest choice.

code_snippets.title: The three metrics in plain Python
code_snippets.explanation: If both vectors are normalized (length = 1), the division in cosine similarity does nothing. `cosine_similarity` and `dot_product` return the same value. `np.dot()` runs faster on hardware because it skips the division.

code_snippets.title: Choosing a metric in pgvector
code_snippets.explanation: pgvector exposes three operators. For normalized OpenAI embeddings, the inner product (`<#>`) is the fastest and gives the same top-k results as cosine. Note: all three return distance, so ORDER BY ascending = most similar first.

common_mistakes.title: Using Euclidean distance on vectors that are not normalized
common_mistakes.explanation: If embedding vectors vary in length, two vectors with identical meaning but different lengths will score poorly under Euclidean distance. Cosine handles this correctly because it ignores length entirely.

common_mistakes.title: Sorting by distance in descending order
common_mistakes.explanation: Vector database operators return distance (smaller = more similar). If you sort descending (`DESC`), you get the most dissimilar vectors first. For similarity search, sort ascending (`ASC`), or use a similarity operator if one is available.

recall_questions.q: Explain the difference between cosine similarity and Euclidean distance to a classmate.
recall_questions.answer: Cosine similarity measures the angle between two vectors — it only cares about direction and ignores length. Euclidean distance measures the physical straight-line gap between two points, which depends on both direction and length.

recall_questions.q: If you use normalized embeddings, why might you configure your database to use dot product instead of cosine similarity?
recall_questions.answer: When vectors are normalized (length = 1), dot product gives the same ranking as cosine similarity but runs faster because it skips the length-division step. The results are identical, so you pay less CPU cost.

recall_questions.q: If vector A and vector B point in exactly the same direction but vector A is twice as long, what is their cosine similarity?
recall_questions.answer: 1 — a perfect match. Cosine ignores vector length entirely and only looks at direction. Identical direction means identical meaning, regardless of magnitude.

recall_questions.q: What happens if you sort pgvector results using the <=> (cosine distance) operator in descending order?
recall_questions.answer: You retrieve the vectors with the highest distance — the least similar ones. Distance operators in pgvector return how far apart two vectors are, so ascending order gives the most similar results. Descending order gives the worst matches.

oa_questions.question: You migrate from an open-source embedding model (variable vector length) to OpenAI's embeddings (normalized to length 1). Your vector database sorts by cosine distance. A coworker suggests switching to dot product to save CPU cycles. Is this safe?
oa_questions.answer: Yes. OpenAI's embeddings are normalized, so all vectors have length 1. For normalized vectors, dot product ranks results in exactly the same order as cosine similarity, but runs faster. You only need to make sure the ORDER BY direction is correct — ascending for both distance metrics.
oa_questions.approach: Identify the relationship between normalization, cosine, and dot product. State clearly that normalization makes them equivalent for ranking, so the switch is safe.

oa_questions.question: Your retrieval system returns the worst possible matches for every query. You are using `ORDER BY embedding <=> query_vector DESC` in pgvector. What is the bug?
oa_questions.answer: The `<=>` operator in pgvector returns cosine distance — smaller values are more similar. Sorting DESC means you are ordering from largest distance to smallest, which gives you the least similar vectors first. Change `DESC` to `ASC` to get the most similar results.
oa_questions.approach: Spot the distance vs similarity inversion. pgvector operators return distance (lower is better), so you must sort ascending for similarity search.
